title: Classification models
summary: Predicting categories with logistic regression, the likelihood and entropy ideas behind cross-entropy loss, softmax for many classes, k-nearest neighbours and Naive Bayes, and support vector machines with soft margins and kernels.
syllabus: Maximum likelihood, entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
NOAI AI/ML: softmax, multi-class vs multi-label, Naive Bayes and Laplace smoothing

lessons.title: Logistic regression
lessons.summary: Squashing a linear score into a probability with the sigmoid, drawing a decision boundary, and the log loss.
objectives: You can compute σ(z) for simple z and interpret it as a probability
You can describe the decision boundary wᵀx + b = 0
You can compute binary cross-entropy and explain why it punishes confident mistakes

concepts.name: Sigmoid turns scores into probabilities
concepts.explain: Logistic regression computes a linear score z = wᵀx + b and squashes it with σ(z) = 1/(1 + e⁻ᶻ) into a number between 0 and 1. σ(0) = 0.5, large positive z gives nearly 1, large negative nearly 0.
concepts.analogy: A dimmer switch that smoothly turns 'how strong the evidence is' into 'how likely it is'.

visual.shows: A 1D dataset of pass/fail against hours studied with the sigmoid curve fitted; the 0.5 threshold point is marked.
visual.interaction: Slide w (steepness) and b (shift); press 'fit' to optimise.
visual.aha: The weight controls how sharp the decision is and the bias controls where it happens.

concepts.name: A linear decision boundary
concepts.explain: In 2D, the set of points where wᵀx + b = 0 is a straight line: on one side the probability is above 0.5, on the other below. The weight vector is perpendicular to the boundary and points towards the positive class.
concepts.analogy: A coastline on a map: one side land, the other sea, with the beach as the 50-50 zone.

visual.shows: Two classes of points with a background coloured by predicted probability, the boundary line and the weight vector arrow.
visual.interaction: Drag the weight arrow to rotate the boundary and change its length to sharpen the probability gradient; drag the bias handle to shift it.
visual.aha: Logistic regression is a linear classifier with a confidence map around the line.

concepts.name: Log loss punishes confident mistakes
concepts.explain: Binary cross-entropy is −log p for a positive example and −log(1 − p) for a negative one. Predicting 0.9 for a true positive costs about 0.105; predicting 0.01 costs about 4.6. Unlike MSE with a sigmoid, it gives strong gradients when the model is confidently wrong.
concepts.analogy: A quiz where being confidently wrong costs far more than saying 'not sure'.

visual.shows: The curve −log p over p from 0 to 1 with a draggable predicted probability and its loss value; the MSE curve is overlaid for comparison.
visual.interaction: Drag p; toggle the true label between 1 and 0.
visual.aha: Cross-entropy explodes as confident predictions turn out wrong, which makes it the right loss for probabilities.

checkpoint_focus: BCE = −[y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)]

lessons.title: Likelihood, entropy and cross-entropy
lessons.summary: Why classifiers are trained with cross-entropy: maximum likelihood, and the information-theory view of surprise.
objectives: You can explain maximum likelihood and why we maximise the log-likelihood
You can compute entropy and cross-entropy for small distributions
You can explain why minimising cross-entropy is maximum likelihood, and that KL divergence is not symmetric

concepts.name: Maximum likelihood
concepts.explain: Likelihood asks: if the parameter were this value, how probable is the data we saw? Maximum likelihood picks the parameter that makes the data most probable. For 7 heads in 10 flips, the likelihood p⁷(1 − p)³ peaks at p = 0.7. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation also multiplies in a prior belief, which acts like regularisation.
concepts.analogy: Guessing a basketball player's shooting accuracy from tonight's shots: the best guess is the accuracy that makes tonight's results least surprising.

visual.shows: A likelihood curve over p ∈ [0, 1] for the observed flips, with its peak marked and the log-likelihood curve underneath.
visual.interaction: Add heads or tails with buttons; drag a p marker to read off the likelihood.
visual.aha: Minimising cross-entropy loss is the same as maximising likelihood, which is why ML uses it.

concepts.name: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
concepts.explain: Entropy H(p) = −Σ p log p measures how unpredictable a distribution is: high for a fair coin, zero for a certain outcome. Cross-entropy H(p, q) measures the cost of predicting with q when the truth is p, and KL divergence = H(p, q) − H(p) is the extra cost; it is never negative and KL(p‖q) usually differs from KL(q‖p).
concepts.analogy: Packing for a trip: if you expect sunshine (q) but it pours (p), you pay a 'surprise cost'; KL is how much worse you did than someone who knew the real forecast.

visual.shows: Two editable bar distributions p and q over four outcomes, with readouts for H(p), H(p, q), KL(p‖q) and KL(q‖p).
visual.interaction: Drag bar heights (auto-normalised); make q match p to see KL drop to 0; swap roles to see asymmetry.
visual.aha: Cross-entropy is minimised when the prediction matches the truth, which is exactly what a classifier's loss rewards.

concepts.name: Losses are negative log-likelihoods
concepts.explain: If you assume Gaussian noise around predictions, maximising likelihood is minimising mean squared error. If outputs are Bernoulli or categorical probabilities, it is minimising cross-entropy. Loss functions are not arbitrary; they come from a probability model.
concepts.analogy: Like choosing a marking scheme that fits the type of answer: numbers get distance-based marking, multiple choice gets right/wrong marking.

visual.shows: Two tabs deriving MSE from a Gaussian and BCE from a Bernoulli, step by step.
visual.interaction: Click through each derivation step with reveal buttons.
visual.aha: MSE and cross-entropy are both maximum likelihood with different noise assumptions.

checkpoint_focus: MLE for a coin (7 heads in 10 → 0.7)
Entropy of a fair coin is 1 bit
Losses as negative log-likelihoods (MSE ↔ Gaussian, CE ↔ categorical)

lessons.title: Softmax, cross-entropy and multi-class problems
lessons.summary: Extending to many classes with softmax, the cross-entropy loss, and the difference between multi-class and multi-label.
objectives: You can compute softmax for small logits
You can compute cross-entropy for a one-hot target
You can choose softmax+CE for multi-class and sigmoid+BCE for multi-label

concepts.name: Softmax turns logits into a distribution
concepts.explain: Softmax exponentiates each score (logit) and divides by the total: pᵢ = e^{zᵢ}/Σⱼ e^{zⱼ}. The outputs are positive and sum to 1, the largest logit gets the largest probability, and adding the same constant to every logit changes nothing. Label smoothing softens the one-hot target (for example 0.9 for the true class and the remaining 0.1 shared among the others), which stops logits growing without bound and usually improves calibration.
concepts.analogy: Splitting a prize pool where each finalist's share grows exponentially with their score.

visual.shows: Draggable logit bars for 4 classes and the resulting probability bars, with exact values.
visual.interaction: Drag logits; press 'add 5 to all' to see probabilities unchanged; slide a temperature divider to sharpen or flatten.
visual.aha: Only differences between logits matter, and softmax magnifies them exponentially.

concepts.name: Multi-class versus multi-label
concepts.explain: Multi-class means exactly one correct label (a digit is 3 or 7, not both), so use softmax with cross-entropy. Multi-label means several labels can be true at once (a photo containing a dog and a cat), so use an independent sigmoid per label with binary cross-entropy.
concepts.analogy: Choosing one CCA (multi-class) versus ticking every subject you like (multi-label).

visual.shows: An output layer with 4 units, an image card with one or several objects, and the probabilities under softmax versus sigmoid heads.
visual.interaction: Toggle the head type and the image; see that softmax forces probabilities to compete while sigmoids do not.
visual.aha: Softmax makes classes compete for probability; sigmoids judge each label independently.

checkpoint_focus: Softmax sums to 1 and is shift-invariant

lessons.title: k-nearest neighbours
lessons.summary: Classifying by a vote of the most similar training examples: choosing k, choosing a distance metric, and why the features must be scaled.
objectives: You can classify a point with k-NN and explain how k changes the boundary
You can compute Euclidean, Manhattan and cosine distance and explain why they can disagree
You can explain why k-NN needs scaled features and is slow at prediction time

concepts.name: Vote of the neighbours
concepts.explain: k-NN stores the training data and, for a new point, finds the k closest training points and takes a majority vote (or the average for regression). There is no training step, but every prediction must compare against all stored points.
concepts.analogy: Deciding which hawker stall is good by asking the 5 people nearest to you in the queue.

visual.shows: A 2D two-class dataset, the background coloured by k-NN prediction, and a draggable query point with circles linking it to its k neighbours.
visual.interaction: Drag the query; slide k from 1 to 25; switch between Euclidean and Manhattan distance.
visual.aha: k = 1 gives jagged islands around every point (overfitting); large k gives smooth, eventually too-simple boundaries.

concepts.name: Distance metrics change neighbourhoods
concepts.explain: Euclidean distance is the straight-line distance; Manhattan distance adds the absolute differences along each axis. Cosine distance compares directions. The choice, and feature scaling, decide which points count as 'near'.
concepts.analogy: As the crow flies versus driving along Singapore's grid of roads.

visual.shows: Around a query point, the set of points within distance r drawn as a circle (Euclidean), diamond (Manhattan) or wedge (cosine), with neighbours highlighted.
visual.interaction: Toggle the metric; drag r; stretch one feature axis to mimic unscaled data.
visual.aha: Neighbourhoods are defined by your metric and your scaling, not by the algorithm.

lessons.title: Naive Bayes and Laplace smoothing
lessons.summary: Bayes' theorem with a bold independence assumption: counting words to classify messages, and adding one to every count.
objectives: You can compute a Naive Bayes score from priors and word likelihoods
You can explain what is naive about Naive Bayes and why it still works
You can apply Laplace smoothing and explain why it is needed

concepts.name: Bayes with independent features
concepts.explain: Naive Bayes scores each class as prior x product of P(feature | class), assuming features are independent given the class. It picks the class with the highest score. Training is just counting.
concepts.analogy: Like guessing whether a message is from your CCA chat by multiplying how typical each word is for that chat.

visual.shows: A message's words as chips; for each class a running product of word likelihood bars times the prior.
visual.interaction: Add or remove words; the class scores and the winner update.
visual.aha: Independence turns one hard probability into many easy ones.

concepts.name: Laplace smoothing
concepts.explain: If a word never appeared in spam during training, its likelihood is 0 and the whole product becomes 0. Adding 1 to every count (Laplace smoothing) keeps unseen words from vetoing a class.
concepts.analogy: Like giving every new dish at least one star so a single missing review does not make it disappear.

visual.shows: Word count tables with and without +1 smoothing and the resulting class scores.
visual.interaction: Include an unseen word and toggle smoothing; see the zero product disappear.
visual.aha: Smoothing prevents a single zero from dominating.

lessons.title: Support vector machines and kernels
lessons.summary: The widest-street classifier, soft margins controlled by C, and the kernel trick for curved boundaries.
objectives: You can explain the maximum-margin idea and support vectors
You can predict the effect of C on the margin
You can explain the kernel trick and the RBF kernel's gamma

concepts.name: The widest street
concepts.explain: Many lines can separate two classes; an SVM picks the one with the widest margin (the empty 'street' between the classes). Only the points on the edge of the street, the support vectors, determine the boundary; moving any other point does not change it.
concepts.analogy: Building a road between two kampongs: make it as wide as possible, and only the houses at the roadside matter.

visual.shows: Two separable classes with the maximum-margin line, the two margin lines and circled support vectors; the margin width is shown.
visual.interaction: Drag points; moving a non-support point leaves the line unchanged, moving a support vector shifts it.
visual.aha: The decision depends only on a few critical points at the edge of the margin.

concepts.name: Soft margins and C
concepts.explain: Real data overlaps, so a soft-margin SVM allows some points inside the street or on the wrong side, each with a penalty. C sets the price of these violations: large C means few violations and a narrow margin (risk of overfitting); small C means a wider margin that tolerates errors.
concepts.analogy: A strict prefect (large C) who allows no exceptions versus a relaxed one (small C) who accepts a few for overall harmony.

visual.shows: Overlapping classes with the margin and violating points highlighted, and counters for margin width and violations.
visual.interaction: Slide C on a log scale; add an outlier to see large C contort the boundary.
visual.aha: C trades margin width against training errors, just like regularisation.

concepts.name: The kernel trick
concepts.explain: Data that no line can separate in 2D may become separable after mapping to more dimensions (for example adding r² = x² + y²). Kernels compute similarity in that bigger space without building it explicitly. The RBF kernel's gamma sets how local each point's influence is: large gamma gives very wiggly boundaries.
concepts.analogy: Two kinds of coins mixed on a table can be separated by flicking the table so the heavier coins bounce higher, then slicing horizontally.

visual.shows: A ring-shaped dataset in 2D and its lifted 3D-style view (drawn as an isometric plot) with a flat separating plane, then the curved boundary it creates back in 2D; an RBF panel shows the boundary for different gamma.
visual.interaction: Slide the lift amount to animate the mapping; slide gamma and C for the RBF SVM.
visual.aha: A straight cut in a richer space is a curved boundary in the original space.

checkpoint_focus: Hard vs soft margin, slack, C
Kernel trick maps to higher dimensions
